questions.prompt: A bank transfer debits Alice and credits Bob. The server crashes between the two updates. Which ACID property guarantees Alice isn't charged without Bob being paid?
questions.explanation: Atomicity means the transaction happens completely or not at all. Durability is about committed data surviving a crash, which is a different guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which workload fits a key-value store best?

options.text: Ad-hoc monthly revenue reports across many tables
Looking up a user's session data by session id on every request
Finding friends of friends who like the same band

questions.explanation: Key-value stores excel at get and put by key. Reports need flexible queries (SQL), and friends-of-friends is a graph traversal.

questions.prompt: In a wide-column store, you need 'the latest 50 messages in a conversation'. What's the natural design?

options.text: Partition by conversation id and sort messages by time within the partition
One table of all messages, then filter by conversation at query time
Store each message under a random key

questions.explanation: Wide-column designs follow the query: one partition per conversation, sorted by time, makes 'latest 50' a single fast read of one partition.

questions.prompt: Which requirements point toward a relational database as the source of truth? Select all that apply.

options.text: Multi-row transactions, such as reserving inventory while creating an order
Queries and reports that will change as the product evolves
Billions of sensor readings per day, always read by device and time
Rules like 'email must be unique' enforced by the database

questions.explanation: Transactions, flexible queries and declared constraints are relational strengths. Very high-volume writes read by one known key and time range suit a partitioned wide-column or time-series store.

questions.prompt: Two transactions under snapshot isolation both check 'at least one doctor on call', then each sets a different doctor off call. Both commit and nobody is on call. What is this, and what prevents it?

options.text: A dirty read; fixed by read committed
Write skew; fixed by serializable isolation or locking the rows read (SELECT … FOR UPDATE)
A lost update; fixed by adding an index

questions.explanation: Each transaction wrote a different row, so no write conflict was detected, but together they broke a rule based on what they read. That's write skew. Serializable isolation or explicit locks on the rows read prevent it.
